replying_to: Replying to Effective Certification of Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models
display_title: Official Review of Paper3898 by Reviewer gsTH

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper deals with verification of a recently introduced type of model, Monotone Operator Equilibrium Models (MonDEQ). 
These models are defined by finding the fixed point of an operator corresponding to the input, and applying a linear transformation to it. 
This fixed point is usually found by operator splitting iterative algorithm.

This paper want to perform verification of MonDEQs models and need to therefore compute on over-approximation of the reachable values (a convex overestimation of the reachable fixed points).
The authors show a theorem (4.1) that if the over-approximation "shrinks" at one iteration, then this guarantees that the fixed point set is included in that approximation.

As a result, they need to have a representation of the over-approximation that allows checking for inclusion.
The authors discuss how to do this using an Hybrid-Zonotope representation.

The resulting algorithm (CRAFT) propagate those zonotope through the iteration of the operator splitting algorithm, checking at each stage whether the overapproximation has started shrinking. Once it has, they have a guarantee that the over-approximation they hold is an overapproximation of the set of fixed point, so they can use that to obtain an over-approximation of the outputs and check for robustness.

Experimental evaluation is performed over MonDEQs  trained on MNIST and CIFAR10.
content.main_review:
# Strengths
The paper is quite clearly written and is very self contained. Even though I did not have more than a passing knowledge of the MonDEQs model, the paper was sufficiently clear in presenting an introduction to them to give enough context. The description of their algorithm was also quite well illustrated, making it possible to follow along.
The contribution are quite novel. Beyond MonDEQ, the algorithm described by the author provide a template to follow when wanting to obtain bounds for an infinite process, in which case there is no possibilty to run standard methods. This is quite interesting and original, in addition to the regular contribution of enabling verification of a new type of model.


# Weaknesses
## Q1: Motivation of the paper.
The abstract of the paper claim "As MonDEQs are inherently robust to adversarial perturbations, investigating new methods to certify their robustness is a promising research direction". A similar claim of "high inherent empirical robustness" is also made in the introduction. This should be justified in some way, because they are not supported by the results visible in the paper.
Picking from Table 1, the MonDEQs used achieve adversarial accuracy of :
83% on MNIST, for eps=0.05
36% on Cifar10, for eps=2/255
Looking for example at the IBP paper (2018) Table 3, it achieved *verified accuracy* (so a stronger requirement) of 
91% on MNIST, for eps=0.3
44% on Cifar10, for eps=2/255.
Given that the robustness results are this far below even simple methods, I think that the claim of "high inherent robustness" should be dialed down or better substantiated.
The fact that those models are also so far beyond the state of the art put also some limitations on how useful the algorithm is. 

## Q2: Guarantees of the paper
I'm wondering about some aspects of the paper which would have implications to the applicability of the algorithm.
- Is there a guarantee that containment will happen (so that we know that Theorem 4.1 will be applicable at some point)?
- If containment happens, is there some guarantees that it is going to be detectable? (Theorem 5.2 says that Z' is contained if, but this is only a sufficient condition)

## Q3: Clarification about choice of iteration.
Is there some reason why the changes of operator splitting algorithm is necessary? I see in Appendix B that PR is run for a few more iterations in the actual implementation. Do the overapproximations of the operator operate differently with regards to the resulting size of the approximations? Is there some trade-offs to 
observe? Or is it simply that Theorem 4.2 is applicable for any choice of alpha, rather than a specific parameter.

## Q4: Clarification about the widening.
The discussion in Appendix B of "Widening" appears problematic, and I'm slightly uncomfortable with it being hidden only in the appendix. Is the idea to increase the size of the feasible domain at one level, and count on the image of that increase domain to be shrinking (so assuming that applying the layer is a contractive operation). Additionally increasing looseness is the opposite of how verification is done (even this paper spends a lot of effort, such as in 5.1 to obtain tighter abstractions) so I think that this point should be highlighted more and discussed more (have an ablation study for it, and be present in the main body of the paper.)

## Typos:
Page 4: At the beginning of the proof of Theorem 4.1, S_i_hat and S_i are defined to be the same. I assume the content of the second one should not have hats.
Page 14: "M-Z3onotop" -> "M-Zonotope"

Side questions:
- In the result of Table 3, could you clarify the difference between the two "No Box Component" line? Does it correspond just to the fact that one is a naive version with default hyperparameters, while the other one is the same method, but with  hyperparameter tuning?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper develops interesting techniques to deal with the particularities of a class of models and shows novel methods to solve the arising problems (infinite depth computation). It presents the algorithm in a clear manner.
At the same time, it appears if you read the appendix that the algorithm that they describe is a much simplified version of what they actually run and it's unclear about what are the necessary conditions for their algorithm to be successful. The robustness results obtained by MonDEQs also seem to be significantly worse than those obtained by traditional CNNs, so the applicability of the method might be limited.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3898 by Reviewer gsTH

content.title: Response to Reviewer gsTH
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful feedback and for raising interesting questions, which we answer below.

**Can you establish the “high inherent empirical robustness” claimed of monDEQs claimed in Abstract/Intro?**  
We note that the key difference to IBP is that the networks there were trained specifically to be amenable to certification by the propagation of interval bounds. Explicit neural networks trained without adversarial augmentations or IBP, perform noticeably worse.
See e.g., Pabbaraju et al., 2021:

“Figure 4b shows the results: in general, over a range of  values,
the robust test accuracy of the monDEQ with m = 20 is larger than that of the DNNs”


**Is containment (Theorem 4.1) guaranteed? Can it always be detected?**  
From the work on Lipschitz bounds, we know that a bounded fixpoint set exists and convergence guarantees show that in the concrete these will be reached for suitably chosen alpha. There is however no guarantee that the corresponding latent state set will ever actually contract. There is also no guarantee that containment is detectable, as our containment check is a sound over-approximation for general M-Zonotopes.
However, empirically we have found that when using PR splitting, we can find containment in almost all evaluated cases (see Table 1).

**Why is the change of operator splitting algorithm necessary?**  
We have found that PR is much more robust with respect to hyper-parameter settings and finding settings for FwBw that converge initially can be very hard, but ultimately yields tighter bounds (see Table 3). Switching allows us to combine the best of both worlds and is enabled by Th. 4.2.

**Can you expand on “widening” and promote its discussion in the paper?**  
A key difference to the standard certification setting is that due to the contractive behaviour of the fixpoint iteration, approximation errors do not necessarily accumulate. Further, widening is only used during the initial phase of certification where we aim to find a contracting latent state; during the second phase, where we aim to certify correct classification it is turned off. We consider this to be more of engineering optimization improving the performance in some settings and hence do not believe it belongs in the main paper.

**In Table 3, what is the difference between the two "No Box Component" lines? Does one use the standard hyperparameters, while the other uses specifically tuned ones?**  
Indeed, one is with default parameters, the other after substantial hyperparameter tuning.

We hope to have been able to answer all of the reviewer’s questions and look forward to the update of their review based on this response.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a verification procedure for Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models that is based on abstract interpretations of the fixpoint operations. In particular, instead of the box domain, the M-Zonotope domain is used which is more precise but still admits scalable inclusion checks.
content.main_review:
The paper introduces a sound technique for verifying monDEQ. The paper is well-written and appears to out-perform existing baselines.
The proposed procedure is reasonable, in order to enable efficient verification, it seems unavoidable to sacrifice both completeness and convergence. 
I am concerned with the choice of the abstraction domain. Another candidate is DeepPoly, which generally provides better empirical results than Zonotopes in traditional neural network verification scenarios can improve the performance. Since a DeepPoly element only has four linear constraints, checking inclusion between two DeepPoly element should also be efficient (e.g., with 4 inexpensive LP calls). I wonder whether the authors have tried to use the DeepPoly domain and what is the motivation for using Zonotope?
Another concern is with the depth of the technical contribution. The abstraction domain is the same as  (Mirman et al., 2018). And the main contribution lies in the inclusion check between two M-Zonotopes and the overall procedure (Algorithm 1), which is specific to monDEQ, a rather niche architecture. 
In conclusion, I think the choice of the abstract domain lacks strong motivations and the depth of the contribution does not warrant a publication at ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: Reasonable procedure for verifying monDEQ, but lacking strong justification for the choice of the abstraction domain and depth in technical contribution.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3898 by Reviewer W8Gd

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a robustness certification algorithm for a special kind of deep equilibrium model (DEQ), namely the monotone DEQ (monDEQ). It borrows zonotope based certification technique for neural network verification (Singh et al, 2018). In monDEQ, the output of the model comes from an iterative solver such as forward-backward splitting. It can be seen as computation with linear and ReLU functions (Eq. 3), so existing zonotope based certification can be applied with some extensions. Some preliminary results are given on a few small monDEQ models with a few hundred neurons.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

1. This paper is the first zonotope based approach for certifying the robustness of monoDEQ models. Zonotopes are often used for certifying feedforward neural networks but they have not been applied to monDEQ models before.

2. The M-zonotope is an extension of existing zonotope abstraction by combining a box with a zonotope. This combination has not been used in previous works, but isn't box a special case of a zonotope? I am not sure if combining a zonotope with a box increases the precision of overapproximation.  I am also not sure how powerful it is compared to the more advanced polytope based approach (DeepPoly, Singh et al. 2019).

3. The paper is overall easy to follow, however, I think proofs should be moved to the appendix.

Weaknesses:

1. Technical novelty is limited, as zonotope based analysis is a mature technique for certifying the robustness of neural networks. The extension of this technique to monDEQ models is relatively straightforward.

2. Experiments section is largely incomplete and comparisons to a few important baselines such as (Revay et al. 2020) and (Pabbaraju et al.) are missing, which are based on certifying Lipschitz constants.  In table 1, none of the baselines (based on Lipschitz constant or SDP) are included (such as Pabbaraju et al.  2021 and Chen et al. 2021).  These should be added. Very limited comparisons are given in Table 2 for only 1 baseline but it seems the results are questionable - the baseline method SemiSDP has a fixed runtime, which probably means that the authors did not terminate the solver correctly and only ran a fix number of iterations.  This is not a fair comparison.

3. It seems the zonotope based approach is not suitable for certifying DEQs and the proposed approach performs poorly compared to results reported by other monDEQ papers.  For example, if you take a look at the model in Figure 4(a) of (Pabbaraju et al.  2021), they have much better certified accuracy (over 90% at eps=0.05 on MNIST and they can also certify very large eps like 0.2) and they are also much faster (no need to do any zonotope analysis).  If using Lipschitz constant can certify the model much better, I feel the use of the zonotope based approach is questionable - since it requires to overapproximate multiple iterations of the solver which is a fundamental limit of these overapproximation based methods.

4. The scope and practicability of this work are very limited - monDEQ itself is still a quite immature model and its performance is quite poor (compared to other SOTA architectures like CNN and Transformers). Even worse, the models studied are very small, and the clean and certified performance is far from the state-of-the-art certified defense methods. So I feel this paper will make a very limited impact on this field.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I feel this paper is mostly like a hammer in search of a nail rather than solving a useful problem. Additionally, the technical novelty is limited and the experiments section still has quite a few things missing (as mentioned above). The zonotope based certification also cannot convincingly outperform existing approaches. Therefore I rate this paper for rejection. Several suggestions to the authors to further improve the contribution of this paper:

1. Extend to regular DEQ models rather than limiting to monDEQ only. monDEQ is too restrictive. Since we are doing point-wise certification, in a DEQ if an input point can converge, it should be possible that the overapproximation can also converge, so the same zonotope/box analysis may also be applied for each specific test point. This allows us to do better than the existing Lipschitz constant based certification since they can be used for monDEQ only.
2. Extend the algorithm to use a more precise abstraction such as DeepPoly (Singh et al., 2019). DeepPoly is one of the most popular approaches for neural network verification and has largely replaced the zonotope based approach used in this paper.
3. Combine training and certification to enlarge the robust radius such as done in (Mirman et al., 2018).

References (that were not cited in the submission):

Singh, Gagandeep, et al. "An abstract domain for certifying neural networks." Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 3.POPL (2019): 1-30.

content.title: Response to Reviewer W8Gd
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback and for raising interesting questions, which we answer below.

**Is the comparison to Chen et al. 2021 unfair? (not included in Table 1; fixed runtime)**  
We compare only on this one network not in order to be unfair or hide details, but rather in order to be fair: We use the exact network introduced by Chen et al. 2021 which they state to be the largest size that their method scales to:

“The size of PSD matrices is a limiting factor for SDP solvers, our models are
practically restricted to networks for which such size can be handled by SDP solvers. For the popular dataset MNIST [37], whose input dimension is 28 ×28 = 784, we are able to apply our model on monDEQs with moderate size implicit layers (87) and report the corresponding computation time.”

The authors are open about this, and it has also been pointed out by reviewers of that work: https://openreview.net/forum?id=m4rb1Rlfdi
The given runtime is what Chen et al. 2021 report as the average across the first 100 test images (the same samples we consider).

**Can you extend to regular DEQ models rather than focusing on monDEQs?**  
Dropping the monotonicity constraint means that the existence and uniqueness of fixpoints are not guaranteed anymore. Thus it is not sufficient anymore to reason about the robustness of those unique points, but rather one needs to consider the exact behaviour of the solver at inference time. While this is generally possible it requires a different approach and will yield weaker guarantees, we hence decided against pursuing this direction.

**Can training and certification be combined to enlarge the robust radiusas done in Mirman et al., 2018?**  
While in itself interesting, we want to highlight that the results in this paper are particularly interesting because we do not use certifiable training. This is of particular interest, as certifiable training generally significantly worsens the performance on unperturbed samples.

We hope to have been able to answer all of the reviewer’s questions, especially regarding the applicability of Lipschitz based methods and are looking forward to a constructive discussion.

**References**  
Chen et al. 2021, Semialgebraic Representation of Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models NeurIPS21  
Mirman et al. 2018, Differentiable Abstract Interpretation for Provably Robust Neural Networks, ICML18

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method to verify monotone deep Equilibrium models. The authors propose to use the Zonotope approximation from Singh et al. 2018 to find over-approximations/relaxation for the implicit layers. They demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on CIFAR10 and MNIST settings.
content.main_review:
Strengths
1. The authors propose a new technique for the verification of monotone deep equilibrium models (monDEQs).

Weaknesses

1. Limited relevance of the problem
* MonDEQs are not used in practical applications. They are not popular among the research community. So verification of monDEQs is not very relevant for the general machine learning community.
* This paper does not address the limitation of current verification systems. But instead gives a simple extension of the current techniques to a small set of models which are not popular. 
* Are there any specific real-world applications where monDEQs are used and thus this system will be helpful?
[comment]: <> (I personally believe that efforts should be spent on addressing limitations of existing verification systems and such papers only add noise to the)

2. Writing is not good
* The paper is not well written and needed multiple passes for understanding. The authors should spend some time re-organising the re-writing it. 
* Suggestion: A brief overview of the algorithm should be first presented and then the different parts should come as needed. For example, I do not see the point of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 until section 5.2. However, you can provide a summary of the algorithm before sec4, as is presented in para one of 5.2.
* Figure 1 is not very clear.
* I believe that Theorem

3. Missing baselines
* The method is not properly motivated and put in the context of works. You have not shown why the current works from verification literature are not directly applicable.
* Why can a linear propagation style algorithm like CROWN not be used here? I would like to see a discussion on that and a comparison to it. This will also help outline the difference of the implicit setting from the fixed layer setting.

4. Incremental technical contribution
* Overall the method seems to be an extension of the Zonotope based verification work (Singh et al. 2018) to the implicit network setting. What is the technical delta over Singh et al. 2018?
* What is the technical delta over Hybrid-zonotope Mirman et al.2018? What is the difference of M-zonotope to Hybrid-zonotope?
* Relevance of m-zonotope over zonotope: Just the zonotope seems to be performing well in Table 3. In fact it seems that ways to tune $\alpha$ should be investigated. What all ways have you tried for this? Are there relevant works in PR literature that explore ways to tune $\alpha$? Have you explored them?
* Relevance of part 1 of algorithm: Overall the algorithm seems to have 2 parts: (i) Finding an over-approximation that contains $Z*$. (ii) shrinking this over-approximation using FB. (ii) is supported by Theorem 4.2 which is a simple result. Can you provide some other baseline for (i)? If you propagate linear constraints using CROWN, will it achieve (i)? Can you provide such a baseline, as it will show the need for Theorem 4.1 and m-zonotope. 

5. Limited experimental validation
* It has become common in verification papers now to verify medium-sized networks. But the networks verified here are very small. Why are results not provided on medium-sized networks like ConvMed?
*  The networks verified here only reach up to 63% accuracy on CIFAR10. So these networks are not relevant. One major point in favour of MonDEQs is that they reach good accuracy on some standard tasks. But here it seems that your method cannot verify those networks.

Questions

1- How did you do the inclusion check for zonotopes in the experiments? 

2- At the start of sec5, you mention that inclusion checks for zonotopes are computationally expensive. Why is (Sadraddini & Tedrake, 2019) cited here? Can you provide the relevant result from (Sadraddini & Tedrake, 2019)?

3- How is step 10 performed? How do you perform this operation of sets? Section 4 only provides a definition that it would be set of all $h(x)$ for all $x \in X$. 

4- How do you perform the ablation with just FB? Do you use FB for line 6 in the algorithm as well? Is that supported by Theorem 4.1?

5- Why is only PR performing so bad? Did you try running it for a longer time? Maybe it hasn't been tuned properly. 

I am willing to increase my rating depending on the authors' response to my concerns.

Minor edits:
1. Fix the line before eq 6 where you have defined both the symbols to be the same.

Baselines are missing, technical delta over some related work is not justified and the experiments are only performed on small networks. All of this further reduces the importance of the method. Therefore I am voting to reject the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer hkzR
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for raising several interesting questions and answer them below.

**Can you clarify the technical contribution over Zonotopes (Singh et al. 2018) and  Hybrid-Zonotopes (Mirman et al. 2018)?**  
As outlined in the paper, neither Hybrid-Zonotopes nor Zonotopes permit efficient inclusion checks (in fact they are co-NP-complete (Kulmburg & Althoff, 2021)). The discussed notions of properness, consolidation and the proposed inclusion check are novel, non-trivial and crucial to our algorithm. For further comparison see the new Appendix C.4.

**Only Zonotope (“No Box component”) in Table 3 seems to work well. Does it work without adaptation? How was the inclusion check performed?**  
This is not a standard Zonotope (as in Singh et al, 2018) but rather an M-Zonotope where we disable the Box component. Thus we still use the inclusion check we propose. We have clarified this in the write-up.

**The networks verified here are very small and don’t reach high accuracies. Why are no results provided on medium-sized networks like ConvMed?**  
Deep Equilibrium Models and in particular their certification are still novel and standard benchmarks for certification have not yet been established, ConvMed for example is a standard feed-forward network and can not simply be translated into a monDEQ. We do use the same network (FC87) as the only other work certifying $\ell_\infty$ robustness, Chen et al., 2021. In contrast to previous works in this setting, we support an order of magnitude larger models. Furthermore, (mon)DEQs are effectively infinitely deep. So, while for example a ConvMed has 3 hidden layers with latent sizes 4096, 2028 and 100, our largest monDEQ could be considered to have infinitely many hidden layers of size 800.

**Why is Sadraddini & Tedrake, 2019 cited for the expense of Zonotope inclusion checks?**  
Theorem 3 shows an approximate containment check. Even this approximate and empirically lossy check becomes challenging in high dimensions (They only evaluate up to d=10 due to performance degradation while we consider d=800). To avoid confusion, we now cite Kulmburg & Althoff, 2021, which more directly shows that exact containment is co-NP-complete. We still discuss Sadraddini & Tedrake, 2019 in Appendix C.4.

**How is step 10 performed?**  
The convex relaxation of a single operator splitting iteration $g^{FB\\#}_{\alpha}$ is composed of operations that are also found in the neural networks, verifiable by Zonotopes (Singh et al, 2018). We thus compose it from the transformers introduced in their work.

**How do you perform the ablation with just Fwd-Bwd? Do you use Fwd-Bwd for line 6 in the algorithm as well? Is that supported by Theorem 4.1?**  
Yes, we use Fwd-Bwd both before and after containment has been found. Theorem 4.1 applies to any splitting operator that converges to the true result. It is thus applicable to both Fwd-Bwd and PR.

**Why is only PR performing so bad? Did you try running it for a longer time? Maybe it hasn't been tuned properly.**  
We have tried to tune it extensively and run it much longer than what is needed for the method we propose.

We hope to have been able to answer all of the reviewer’s questions and are looking forward to a constructive discussion.

**References**  
Chen et al. 2021, Semialgebraic Representation of Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models NeurIPS21  
Sadraddini & Tedrake 2019, Linear encodings for polytope containment problems, IEEE CDC19

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
$\newcommand{Ro}{\textcolor{orange}{hkzR}}$
$\newcommand{Rt}{\textcolor{green}{W8Gd}}$
$\newcommand{Rth}{\textcolor{blue}{91s6}}$
$\newcommand{Rf}{\textcolor{purple}{gsTH}}$

We thank all reviewers for their insightful questions and valuable feedback. We are particularly encouraged that they consider the tackled problem interesting ($\Rf$), our approach both novel ($\Rt$, $\Rf$) and general ($\Rf$), and our paper well-written and easy to follow ($\Rt$, $\Rth$, $\Rf$). 

Below we answer common questions, before providing more detailed answers in individual responses to every reviewer.

**monDEQs seem to be a relatively niche architecture, why investigate them rather than the fundamental limitations of current verification systems? ($\Ro$, $\Rt$, $\Rth$, $\Rf$)**  
(mon)DEQs represent an interesting and novel network architecture, which has been widely studied, given how recent the idea is (Bai et al. 2019, Bai et al. 2020, Winston et al, 2020, Chen et al. 2021, Pabbaraju et al. 2021, Revay et al. 2020). While we focus on monDEQs in this submission, we believe our approach to be a stepping stone to more general DEQ models, implicit network architectures, and general fixpoint problems. Furthermore, (mon)DEQ, in contrast to conventional architectures, do not need to be trained specifically for robustness to exhibit robustness, which might enable the fundamental limitations of provably trained models, namely their significantly reduced standard accuracy, to be lifted.

**Is CRAFT just a straight-forward extension of Zonotope verification to monDEQs? ($\Ro$, $\Rt$, $\Rth$)**  
No. 

The extension of methods applied to feed forward networks is highly non-trivial: First, we do not simply verify the solver behaviour (which could be done by unrolling its iterations) but the actual mathematical fixpoints, a much stronger result only enabled by our analysis in Section 4. Second, an abstract domain that is not only precise but also enables both efficient inclusion checks *and* propagation through many solver iterations needed to be constructed since none of the typically used ones fulfils these requirements. We added appendix C.4 discussing why existing choices, such as Box, standard Zonotope and Linear Bounds (DeepPoly, CROWN) do not work.

**Why do you not compare against Pabbaraju et al. 2021 and Revay et al. 2020? Don’t they obtain stronger results? ($\Rt$)**  
Both these works consider $\ell_2$-Lipschitz constants and therefore $\ell_2$ robustness. Revay et al. 2020 do not consider certifiable but only empirical robustness and are hence incomparable. We do intentionally not use their more heavily regularized networks to investigate the inherent robustness of monDEQs. Further it can be shown that a certificate for an $\ell_2$-ball yields a certificate for an $\ell_\infty$ ball with a radius of $r_\infty = r_2 / \sqrt{d}$, where d is the input dimension. When this is taken into account, Pabbaraju et al. 2021 obtain much smaller robustness radii.

**Why can’t CROWN-style algorithms be used? Can CROWN be used to find an over-approximation** $Z^*$ **containing the fixpoint set? ($\Ro$, $\Rt$, $\Rth$)**  
While for algorithms like CROWN or DeepPoly an inclusion check can be performed in polynomial time (in terms of latent space and input dimension), the required backsubsitution becomes infeasible as the runtime is quadratic in the number of layers (or iteration steps in the case of a monDEQ) which is much larger (up to 500) than considered even in the most scalable implementations (Müller, et al. 2021). So while these algorithms are in principle applicable, the combination of the inclusion check cost scaling with both input and latent space dimension with the cost of backsubsitution makes their application expensive even for small models. We leave approaches exploring how these restrictions might be lifted to future work and have added a discussion in appendix C.4.

**References**  
Bai et al. 2019, Deep Equilibrium Models, NeurIPS19  
Bai et al. 2020, Multiscale Deep Equilibrium Models, NeurIPS20  
Winston et al, 2020, Monotone operator equilibrium networks, NeurIPS20  
Chen et al. 2021, Semialgebraic Representation of Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models NeurIPS21  
Pabbaraju et al. 2021, Estimating Lipschitz constants of monotone deep equilibrium models, ICLR21
